title: Chunking and Indexing Strategies
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Chunking and Indexing Strategies ##### The function that lost its signature A developer-tools startup in Pune indexed their Python SDK documentation and source for a code-assistant. Retrieval on conceptual questions was fine. Retrieval on "how do I call `create_batch_job`?" returned nothing useful. The chunk containing that function's body existed. It read: ``` payload = {"items": items, "priority": priority} response = self._post("/v2/batch", json=payload) return BatchJob.from_response(response) ``` No function name. No docstring. No class context. A 400-character recursive splitter had cut cleanly through the middle of a method, and the fragment that survived had no lexical or semantic connection to the query. They switched to AST-aware chunking — split at function and class boundaries, prepend the module path and class name to every chunk. Retrieval accuracy on API questions went from 41% to 88%. **Chunking is not a preprocessing detail. It determines what is findable.** Day 33's beginner article covered overlap; today is about matching the strategy to the document type, and about indexing structures that go beyond one-vector-per-chunk. ##### The chunking spectrum ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Document"] --> B{"Structure available?"} B -->|"Code"| C["AST-aware:
function/class boundaries"] B -->|"Markdown / HTML"| D["Heading hierarchy,
then recursive"] B -->|"PDF with layout"| E["Layout-aware:
sections, tables separate"] B -->|"Chat / transcript"| F["Turn-aware, speaker-grouped"] B -->|"Plain prose"| G{"Topic shifts matter?"} G -->|Yes| H["Semantic chunking"] G -->|No| I["Recursive character"] C --> J["Enrich with context header"] D --> J E --> J F --> J H --> J I --> J ``` | Strategy | Cost | Best for | Weakness | |---|---|---|---| | **Fixed size** | Free | Uniform text | Cuts mid-sentence | | **Recursive** | Free | General prose | Ignores document structure | | **Semantic** | Embedding calls | Topic-shifting narrative | Slow, variable sizes | | **Structural** | Free–cheap | Code, markdown, legal | Needs a parser | | **LLM-based** | Expensive | Small high-value corpora | Cost, non-determinism | ##### Semantic chunking Split where the *meaning* shifts rather than at a character count. Embed each sentence, measure the distance between consecutive sentences, and break at the peaks. ```python import re import numpy as np from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer def semantic_chunk(text, embedder, buffer=1, percentile=90, min_chunk_chars=200, max_chunk_chars=2000): """Break where consecutive-sentence similarity drops sharply.""" sentences = [s.strip() for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?।])\s+", text) if s.strip()] if len(sentences) < 3: return [text] # Combine each sentence with its neighbours for a more stable embedding combined = [] for i in range(len(sentences)): lo, hi = max(0, i - buffer), min(len(sentences), i + buffer + 1) combined.append(" ".join(sentences[lo:hi])) emb = embedder.encode(combined, normalize_embeddings=True, batch_size=64) distances = [1 - float(emb[i] @ emb[i + 1]) for i in range(len(emb) - 1)] threshold = float(np.percentile(distances, percentile)) chunks, current = [], [sentences[0]] for i, d in enumerate(distances): current_len = sum(len(s) for s in current) should_break = (d > threshold and current_len >= min_chunk_chars) \ or current_len >= max_chunk_chars if should_break: chunks.append(" ".join(current)) current = [sentences[i + 1]] else: current.append(sentences[i + 1]) if current: chunks.append(" ".join(current)) return chunks ``` **The buffer is what makes this work.** Embedding single sentences produces noisy similarity — pronouns, short sentences, and list items all embed poorly. Combining each sentence with one neighbour on each side smooths the signal substantially. **Note the Devanagari danda `।`** in the sentence splitter. A regex with only `[.!?]` silently treats an entire Hindi paragraph as one sentence, which is a quiet and consequential bug for Indic corpora. **Semantic chunking costs one embedding pass over every sentence in your corpus** — meaningful at ingestion but a one-time cost. It helps most on narrative documents with genuine topic shifts, and barely at all on structured reference material where headings already mark the boundaries. ##### Structural chunking When the document has structure, use it. This is the highest-return chunking work and it is usually cheap. **Code**, via the AST: ```python import ast def chunk_python_file(source: str, module_path: str, max_chars=2000): """Split at function and class boundaries; preserve signatures and context.""" try: tree = ast.parse(source) except SyntaxError: return [{"text": source, "metadata": {"module": module_path, "parse_error": True}}] lines = source.split("\n") chunks = [] def emit(node, class_name=None): start = node.lineno - 1 end = getattr(node, "end_lineno", node.lineno) body = "\n".join(lines[start:end]) qualname = f"{module_path}.{class_name}.{node.name}" if class_name \ else f"{module_path}.{node.name}" docstring = ast.get_docstring(node) or "" header = f"# {qualname}\n" if class_name: header += f"# Method of class {class_name}\n" chunks.append({ "text": header + body[:max_chars], "metadata": { "module": module_path, "qualname": qualname, "kind": type(node).__name__, "class": class_name, "has_docstring": bool(docstring), "start_line": node.lineno, }, }) for node in tree.body: if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)): emit(node) elif isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef): for item in node.body: if isinstance(item, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)): emit(item, class_name=node.name) return chunks ``` **The `# {qualname}` header is the Pune fix.** A chunk that begins `# sdk.batch.BatchClient.create_batch_job` matches the query lexically *and* semantically, where the bare body matched neither. For other languages, `tree-sitter` provides the same capability across dozens of grammars. **Markdown**, via the heading hierarchy: ```python from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter def chunk_markdown(text, chunk_size=900, overlap=120): header_splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter( headers_to_split_on=[("#", "h1"), ("##", "h2"), ("###", "h3")], strip_headers=False, ) body_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=chunk_size, chunk_overlap=overlap, separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", "। ", " ", ""], ) out = [] for section in header_splitter.split_text(text): trail = " > ".join(v for k, v in section.metadata.items() if k.startswith("h")) for piece in body_splitter.split_documents([section]): piece.page_content = f"[{trail}]\n\n{piece.page_content}" piece.metadata["heading_trail"] = trail out.append(piece) return out ``` **Tables must never be split mid-row.** Extract them whole and store them separately, with a generated text summary for embedding: ```python def index_table(table_markdown, caption, llm): """Store the table whole; embed a description of it.""" summary = llm(f"Describe in 2 sentences what this table contains, including " f"its columns and what a reader could look up in it:\n\n" f"{table_markdown[:2000]}") return { "embed_text": f"{caption}\n{summary}", # what gets embedded "return_text": table_markdown, # what gets returned "metadata": {"kind": "table", "caption": caption}, } ``` ##### Multi-vector indexing The generalisation of "embed one thing, return another." **One document, several vectors, each capturing a different way it might be queried.** ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Source chunk"] --> B["Vector 1:
raw chunk text"] A --> C["Vector 2:
LLM summary"] A --> D["Vector 3-5:
hypothetical questions"] A --> E["Vector 6:
extracted keywords"] B --> F[("Index — all vectors
point to the same chunk")] C --> F D --> F E --> F F --> G["Retrieve → dedupe by
source chunk → return chunk"] ``` ```python import uuid import json class MultiVectorIndex: """Multiple embeddings per chunk, all resolving to the same source.""" def __init__(self, vectorstore, llm): self.vs = vectorstore self.llm = llm self.docs: dict[str, dict] = {} def _summarize(self, text): return self.llm( f"Summarise this passage in 2 sentences, preserving key terms, " f"numbers, and identifiers:\n\n{text[:2500]}") def _hypothetical_questions(self, text, n=3): raw = self.llm( f"Generate {n} distinct questions this passage fully answers. " f'Return JSON: {{"questions": ["...", ...]}}\n\n{text[:2500]}') try: return json.loads(raw)["questions"][:n] except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError): return [] def add_chunks(self, chunks, use_summary=True, use_questions=True): ids, texts, metas = [], [], [] for chunk in chunks: doc_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) self.docs[doc_id] = chunk ids.append(f"{doc_id}::raw") texts.append(chunk["text"]) metas.append({**chunk.get("metadata", {}), "doc_id": doc_id, "view": "raw"}) if use_summary: ids.append(f"{doc_id}::sum") texts.append(self._summarize(chunk["text"])) metas.append({**chunk.get("metadata", {}), "doc_id": doc_id, "view": "summary"}) if use_questions: for j, q in enumerate(self._hypothetical_questions(chunk["text"])): ids.append(f"{doc_id}::q{j}") texts.append(q) metas.append({**chunk.get("metadata", {}), "doc_id": doc_id, "view": "question"}) self.vs.upsert(ids=ids, documents=texts, metadatas=metas) def retrieve(self, query, k=5, fetch_k=25): res = self.vs.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=fetch_k, include=["metadatas", "distances"]) seen, out = set(), [] for meta, dist in zip(res["metadatas"][0], res["distances"][0]): did = meta["doc_id"] if did in seen: continue seen.add(did) out.append({**self.docs[did], "score": 1 - dist, "matched_view": meta["view"]}) if len(out) >= k: break return out ``` **Hypothetical-question indexing is the highest-value view.** Users ask questions; documents contain statements. Embedding a question-shaped representation of each chunk closes that asymmetry directly, and it is often worth more than a better embedding model. **`matched_view` is a useful diagnostic.** If most retrievals match on the question view, your raw chunks embed poorly and the questions are carrying the system. If they match on raw, the extra views may not be earning their ingestion cost. **The cost is real**: one or two LLM calls per chunk at ingestion, plus 3–6× the vector storage. Worth it for high-value corpora; excessive for a large low-value one. ##### RAPTOR Hierarchical indexing for questions that require synthesis across many chunks — "what are the main themes in these 400 support tickets?" No individual chunk answers that, so flat retrieval cannot. **RAPTOR** (Sarthi et al., 2024) builds a tree: cluster chunks, summarise each cluster, cluster the summaries, summarise again, recursively. Then index every level. ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture from sklearn.decomposition import PCA def build_raptor_tree(chunks, embedder, llm, max_levels=3, reduce_dim=32, max_clusters=12): """Recursive clustering and summarisation. Returns all nodes across levels.""" all_nodes = [{"text": c["text"], "level": 0, "metadata": c.get("metadata", {})} for c in chunks] current = [c["text"] for c in chunks] for level in range(1, max_levels + 1): if len(current) <= 2: break emb = embedder.encode(current, normalize_embeddings=True) if emb.shape[1] > reduce_dim and len(current) > reduce_dim: emb = PCA(n_components=reduce_dim, random_state=42).fit_transform(emb) n_clusters = min(max_clusters, max(2, len(current) // 4)) gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=n_clusters, random_state=42, covariance_type="full") labels = gmm.fit_predict(emb) summaries = [] for c in range(n_clusters): members = [current[i] for i in range(len(current)) if labels[i] == c] if not members: continue joined = "\n\n---\n\n".join(m[:1200] for m in members[:10]) summary = llm( f"Write a detailed summary of these related passages. Preserve " f"specific facts, numbers, and names. 200 words maximum.\n\n{joined}") summaries.append(summary) all_nodes.append({ "text": summary, "level": level, "metadata": {"n_children": len(members), "cluster": c}, }) current = summaries return all_nodes def index_raptor(nodes, vectorstore, embedder): """Index every level in one collection — 'collapsed tree' retrieval.""" vectorstore.upsert( ids=[f"raptor::L{n['level']}::{i}" for i, n in enumerate(nodes)], documents=[n["text"] for n in nodes], metadatas=[{**n["metadata"], "level": n["level"]} for n in nodes], ) ``` **Collapsed-tree retrieval — indexing all levels in one collection — outperforms tree traversal** in the original paper and is far simpler. A specific question naturally matches a level-0 leaf; a thematic question matches a level-2 summary. The retriever picks the right granularity without you routing it. **GMM rather than K-Means** because soft clustering lets a chunk belong to multiple clusters, which is realistic — a paragraph about pricing and delivery belongs in both themes. **Cost:** roughly `n_chunks / 4` LLM calls per level. For 10,000 chunks over three levels that is around 3,000 calls at ingestion. Substantial but one-time, and it is the only approach here that handles genuinely global questions. ##### Contextual retrieval Anthropic's 2024 technique, and the best cost-to-benefit ratio of anything in this article. Prepend an LLM-generated context sentence to each chunk before embedding. ```python CONTEXTUALIZE = """ {document} Here is a chunk from that document: {chunk} Write a short sentence (under 40 words) situating this chunk within the document, to improve search retrieval. Answer with only that sentence.""" def contextualize_chunks(document_text, chunks, llm, max_doc_chars=100_000): """Prepend document-aware context to each chunk before embedding.""" doc = document_text[:max_doc_chars] out = [] for chunk in chunks: context = llm(CONTEXTUALIZE.format(document=doc, chunk=chunk["text"])) out.append({ **chunk, "embed_text": f"{context.strip()}\n\n{chunk['text']}", "return_text": chunk["text"], "metadata": {**chunk.get("metadata", {}), "context": context.strip()}, }) return out ``` Anthropic reported a ~35% reduction in retrieval failures, rising to ~49% combined with BM25. **Use prompt caching on the document prefix** — the document is identical across all its chunks, so a cached prefix makes this dramatically cheaper than it looks. ##### Evaluating indexing strategies ```python def evaluate_index(index_fn, eval_set, embedder, k=5): """eval_set: [{'query': str, 'relevant_ids': set}]""" import numpy as np import time t0 = time.perf_counter() index = index_fn() build_time = time.perf_counter() - t0 recalls, mrrs, latencies = [], [], [] for item in eval_set: t1 = time.perf_counter() hits = index.retrieve(item["query"], k=k) latencies.append((time.perf_counter() - t1) * 1000) ids = [h["metadata"].get("source_id") for h in hits] rel = item["relevant_ids"] recalls.append(len(set(ids) & rel) / max(len(rel), 1)) mrrs.append(next((1 / r for r, i in enumerate(ids, 1) if i in rel), 0.0)) return { "build_time_s": round(build_time, 1), f"recall@{k}": round(float(np.mean(recalls)), 3), "MRR": round(float(np.mean(mrrs)), 3), "p95_query_ms": round(float(np.percentile(latencies, 95)), 1), } ``` A representative comparison on technical documentation: | Strategy | recall@5 | MRR | Build time | Index size | |---|---|---|---|---| | Fixed 500, no overlap | 0.58 | 0.44 | 12s | 1.0× | | Recursive 800/150 | 0.71 | 0.59 | 14s | 1.1× | | + heading trail | 0.79 | 0.68 | 15s | 1.1× | | Semantic | 0.76 | 0.64 | 210s | 1.0× | | **Contextual retrieval** | **0.87** | **0.76** | 890s | 1.1× | | Multi-vector (+questions) | 0.86 | 0.79 | 1400s | 4.2× | | RAPTOR (collapsed) | 0.81 | 0.70 | 2100s | 1.3× | **Contextual retrieval wins on quality per unit of index size**, and the heading trail — free — gets you most of the way there. RAPTOR's number understates it, because this eval set has few genuinely global questions; on thematic questions it dominates. ##### Document-type recommendations The assignment asks for this mapping: | Document type | Strategy | Chunk size | Key detail | |---|---|---|---| | **Code** | AST / tree-sitter | Whole function | Prepend qualname and class | | **API docs** | Structural + hypothetical questions | 400–800 | Index each endpoint separately | | **Legal contracts** | Clause-level | Whole clause | Preserve clause numbers in metadata | | **Research papers** | Section-aware | 800–1200 | Handle figures and tables separately | | **Chat logs** | Turn-grouped by session | 5–15 turns | Keep speaker labels; window by time | | **Support tickets** | Whole ticket | Variable | RAPTOR for thematic questions | | **Financial reports** | Layout-aware | Section | Tables extracted whole | | **Wikis** | Markdown headings | 800–1200 | Heading trail prefix | | **Transcripts** | Semantic | 1000–1500 | Speaker turns as soft boundaries | | **Indic-language docs** | Recursive with `।` separator | 800–1200 | Multilingual embedder; NFC normalise | ##### Common mistakes - **Splitting code by character count**, destroying signatures and context — the Pune failure. - **No context header**, leaving chunks unintelligible in isolation. - **Splitting tables mid-row.** - **Sentence splitters without the Devanagari danda** for Indic text. - **Semantic chunking on structured documents** where headings already mark boundaries. - **`fetch_k = k`** in multi-vector retrieval, so deduplication leaves too few results. - **RAPTOR without genuinely global questions** in your workload — paying build cost for nothing. - **Contextual retrieval without prompt caching**, making it 10× more expensive than necessary. - **One strategy for a mixed corpus.** Code, prose, and tables need different treatment. - **Never measuring.** Chunking choices are cheap to test and expensive to get wrong. - **Uniform chunk size across document types** because it is one config value. ##### Hands-on: compare on your own corpus Your practical task compares fixed, recursive, and semantic chunking with retrieval quality measured for each. Use the same embedding model and top-k throughout so the only variable is chunking. Then add the heading-trail prefix to your recursive variant — it is free and it usually beats semantic chunking, which is a useful and slightly deflating result to discover yourself. The mini project implements a RAPTOR-style hierarchical index and compares it to flat chunking on multi-hop questions. **Write the eval set to include genuinely global questions** — "what are the recurring themes?" — because on specific factual questions RAPTOR offers little. The comparison is only meaningful if the question distribution includes the cases RAPTOR is built for. The assignment writes a chunking guide mapping document types to approaches. Ground each recommendation in a measurement where you can, and be specific about the *why*: code needs AST chunking because function boundaries are semantic boundaries and signatures carry the retrieval signal, not because it is a best practice. That reasoning is what makes a guide useful to someone facing a document type you did not cover. ##### Key takeaways - **Chunking determines what is findable.** A code chunk without its function signature is unretrievable regardless of embedding quality. - **Use document structure when it exists** — AST for code, headings for markdown, clauses for contracts — and prepend a context header so every chunk is self-describing. - **Embed one thing, return another.** Multi-vector indexing with hypothetical questions closes the question-versus-statement asymmetry directly. - **Contextual retrieval has the best cost-to-benefit ratio** of the advanced techniques, especially with prompt caching on the document prefix. - **RAPTOR is the only approach here that handles genuinely global questions** — build it when your users ask thematic questions, and skip it when they do not.
